subject: Follow-up: unit accounting — tokens vs characters vs requests + caching

Hi Anna / Samir,

Thanks again for the call earlier — great conversation and useful product-fit signals. I promised a short, pragmatic note to make the unit economics discussion less fuzzy. Below is a compact reference we use internally + suggested next steps so we can lock an anchor for procurement.

Quick TL;DR (can skip to examples):
- Tokens = our primary billing unit (input tokens + generated tokens).
- Characters = less precise; useful for rough estimates but not how we bill.
- Requests = API calls; we can charge per-request in special contracts but default is per-token.
- Prompt caching can materially reduce your CPU cost and, in many cases, the billed tokens — but whether it reduces billed tokens depends on how responses are served (cache hit vs partial reuse).

Concrete examples (realistic sizing):
- Example A: short prompt (200 tokens) + model reply (~800 tokens) => billed tokens ≈ 1,000 tokens for that call.
- Example B: long system + prompt (1,200 tokens) + short reply (200 tokens) => billed tokens ≈ 1,400.
- If you have repeated identical prompts and we serve a full cache hit (we return stored response without re-running the model), billed tokens for that call can be reduced to our configured cache retrieval unit (often very small or zero depending on contract).

How caching plays with billing (practical rules of thumb):
- Cache hit (full response returned): no model compute run — billed tokens can be zero or a nominal retrieval fee depending on your contract.
- Cache partial reuse (prefix/KV cache): we still run the model for the uncached suffix; billed tokens include the tokens actually processed by the model.
- Cache scope matters: prompt-level caching (exact prompt match) is the most effective; semantic or fuzzy caching reduces compute but usually still costs tokens for re-generation.

Suggested next steps from here:
1) Can you share a sample 2-week traffic slice (volume of distinct requests by endpoint + avg prompt size + avg reply size)? A spreadsheet with three rows (endpoint, avg_input_tokens, avg_output_tokens) is perfect.
2) I’ll run a back-of-envelope anchor and return a $/1M token target that maps to the budget range you gave on the call.
3) If you want caching to be a gating factor for procurement, we can add a contract clause that enumerates cache-hit billing behavior.

Attachments: i) quick pricing anchor worksheet (redwood-pricing-anchor.xlsx) ii) brief diagram showing prefix vs full-response caching (prompt-caching-diagram.png)

Thanks — happy to hop on a quick 20-min follow-up if useful.

Best,

Anna — great questions, answered inline below. I’m copying Neha (pricing) so she can confirm contract-level behaviors and the rounded anchors.

1) Token counting and rounding:
- We use our tokenizer counts (the same one we show in the pricing docs). We do not arbitrarily round up to large buckets by default; billed tokens = tokenized_input + tokenized_output.
- We do support minimum-billing thresholds in enterprise deals (e.g., min 50 tokens per request) if you want easier per-request math for procurement. That’s a configurable clause in Dedicated/Private contracts.

2) Prefix + mutable suffix patterns:
- Prefix caching is effective if the large portion of the prompt is identical across calls (the part we cache). In your two-step flow: we can cache the common prefix and then only run the model for the appended mutable suffix. Billed tokens will include whatever tokens the model processes at serving time (so if cached prefix avoids re-processing 1,000 tokens, you save those tokens on cache hits).
- Important: if the mutable suffix causes the model to generate a different-length response, you still pay for the generated tokens. But the bulk prompt cost can be avoided with cache hits.

3) Requests -> tokens -> $ example (worked):
- Suppose you estimate 500k requests/month. 
- If avg_input_tokens = 300 and avg_output_tokens = 700, avg tokens/request = 1,000.
- Monthly tokens = 500k * 1,000 = 500M tokens/month.
- If target price = $1,200 per 1M tokens, monthly spend = 500 * $1,200 = $600k/month.
- If you prefer to keep "requests/month" for procurement simplicity, we can convert anchor points like above and provide the equivalent requests-based commitment band (e.g., 250k–750k requests/month maps to $X monthly commit given your avg tokens/request).

Neha — can you confirm the default cache-hit billing behavior for enterprise deals (is full-response cache served without token billing or do we bill a nominal retrieval unit)?

Next step: Anna / Samir — if you can drop a small CSV (1,000 rows) or the summarized three-row spreadsheet I mentioned, I’ll run a sampling anchor and return a $/1M token suggestion and a conservative worst-case estimate (no caching), plus a best-case w/ estimated cache hit rate.

Best,
Ben
